summary: A survey of which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP, this edition run in February 1983. It continues a series by David Smallberg. Replaced by RFC 847.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on every computer's door to see which would answer. This is one week's tally.

subtitle: An early snapshot of TCP adoption across ARPANET hosts

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET developers needed to know which hosts had implemented and deployed the new TCP protocol for standard services like Telnet, FTP and SMTP.
tldr.mechanism: The survey probed 325 known ARPANET hosts from a single source host between 22 and 23 February 1983, testing whether each would accept TCP connections for three services and recording the results.
tldr.outcome: The results showed widespread adoption of TCP across the ARPANET: 181 hosts accepted Telnet (77%), 173 accepted FTP (74%), and 157 accepted SMTP (67%). Replaced by RFC 847, which repeated the survey for April 1983.

today: RFC 846 is an Internet Standard historical document. It has been superseded by RFC 847, which repeated the survey in April 1983 with updated results. Neither survey is actively used; they serve as a snapshot of TCP adoption during the early transition from NCP to TCP on the ARPANET.

sections.title: Introduction and Methodology
sections.content:
This RFC documents a survey conducted on 22 February 1983 (with retries on 23 February) by David Smallberg to determine which hosts on the ARPANET accepted TCP connections for three important network services: Telnet (remote terminal access), FTP (file transfer), and SMTP (electronic mail transmission).

The survey was performed from a single source host, ISI-VAXA.ARPA, testing 325 hosts listed in the NIC hostname table as of 18 February 1983. Each host was classified in the NIC table by what services it claimed to support (marked as T for TCP, t for Telnet, f for FTP, s for SMTP, or combinations thereof). The survey results showed which of these claims were accurate.
sections.eli5: One person sat at a computer and tried to call every computer they knew about to see if it would let them in using TCP. They tested three different types of calls: remote login, file sharing, and mail.

sections.title: Summary Statistics
sections.content:
Out of 325 hosts tested, the survey found substantial TCP adoption. For Telnet, 181 hosts (56%) accepted connections (from hosts claiming Telnet support, 77% worked as claimed). For FTP, 173 hosts (53%) accepted connections (78% of those claiming FTP support). For SMTP, 157 hosts (48%) accepted connections (67% of those claiming SMTP support).

In each category, some hosts were unreachable, some refused the connection, and some were dead or not responding. The survey also documented that a small number of hosts offered FTP with anonymous user access (14 hosts), allowing guest logins without authentication.

The variation in acceptance rates across the three services reflects differences in implementation maturity: terminal access protocols were most mature, file transfer protocols less so, and mail systems had the lowest adoption.
sections.eli5: Most computers on the network would let you log in remotely, a lot would let you get files, and fewer would take your mail. Some didn't even answer.

sections.title: Data Organization and Results Format
sections.content:
The RFC presents results in two formats. The first shows all 325 hosts in alphabetical order, listing each host's IP address, what the NIC claimed it supported, and whether it actually accepted connections for Telnet, FTP, and SMTP. Each result was marked as accepted (worked), accepted+ (FTP allowed anonymous guest access), refused (rejected the connection), unreachable (network path down), or dead (host not responding).

The second listing reorganizes the same hosts by network number (the initial octets of their IP address), which allows reading the results organized by ARPANET subnet or organization. This dual presentation helps network administrators understand both the overall landscape and the adoption by their own institution.
sections.eli5: The results are listed two ways: alphabetically by computer name, and by network address. Both show what worked and what didn't.

sections.title: Significance and Implications
sections.content:
This survey captures a critical moment in ARPANET history. In 1983, TCP was relatively new (RFC 793, published in 1981), and the network still ran on older NCP (Network Control Protocol) software on many hosts. This snapshot documents the transition mid-flight: most major research institutions and military networks had deployed TCP, but deployment was far from universal.

The survey identifies specific gaps: some institutions with only TCP claims had zero acceptance, while major technology centers like CMU, Stanford, MIT, and UC Berkeley showed consistently high adoption. The presence of 63 completely dead hosts and 7 unreachable networks indicates network infrastructure challenges and highlights why such surveys were valuable to network operators planning migration strategies.
sections.eli5: This shows when TCP was new and most computers didn't have it yet. It helped network managers understand what actually worked in the real world, not just what people said they had.
